title: Ch 5 — Mass & Energy Analysis of Control Volumes
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 5
description: Mass conservation, flow work, the steady-flow energy equation, and devices.

cards.front: Write the *mass flow rate* through a cross-section.
cards.back: $\dot{m} = \rho V A = \dfrac{V A}{v}$, with V the average velocity, A the area and v the specific volume. Volume flow rate $\dot{V} = V A$.
$\sum_{in}\dot{m} = \sum_{out}\dot{m}$. For a single stream, $\dot{m}_1 = \dot{m}_2$, i.e. $\rho_1 A_1 V_1 = \rho_2 A_2 V_2$.
The work needed to push a unit mass of fluid across the control-volume boundary: $w_{flow} = Pv$.

cards.front: Why does enthalpy appear in the energy of a flowing fluid?
cards.back: The energy of a flowing fluid per unit mass is $\theta = h + \dfrac{V^2}{2} + gz$, where $h = u + Pv$ already bundles internal energy with the flow work $Pv$.

cards.front: Single-stream steady-flow energy equation (per unit mass)?

cards.back: Assume $\dot{Q}\approx0$, $\dot{W}=0$, $\Delta PE\approx0$. Then $h_1 + \dfrac{V_1^2}{2} = h_2 + \dfrac{V_2^2}{2}$ — enthalpy is traded for kinetic energy (nozzle accelerates, diffuser decelerates).
Usually $\Delta KE,\,\Delta PE\approx0$ and adiabatic, so $w = h_1 - h_2$. A turbine produces work (w > 0); a compressor/pump consumes it (w < 0).
It is essentially isenthalpic: $h_1 \approx h_2$ (no work, ~adiabatic, negligible ΔKE/ΔPE). Pressure drops sharply; for real gases the temperature usually drops too (Joule–Thomson).

Both have no work and ~no pressure drop. A heat exchanger transfers heat between separate streams; a mixing chamber combines streams into one. Solve with mass + energy balances (include $\dot{Q}$ if heat crosses the chosen boundary).
